title: Detection Use Case Management
summary: Detection use case management is the discipline of running detection content as a managed product rather than a collection of ad hoc rules. It covers the lifecycle of a use case: deriving a detection requirement from threat intelligence, incident lessons or control gaps, documenting the behaviour and the data sources it needs, writing and testing the logic against sample or replayed data, deploying it with an owner and a response procedure, then measuring its health through alert volume, false positive rate and coverage, and finally retiring or rewriting it. In real environments it appears as a use case register or backlog, change controlled deployment, and coverage maps showing which adversary techniques have no detection at all. The mistake teams make is counting rules as a measure of maturity: a large rule set with no owner, no test data and no tuning produces alert fatigue, while a smaller set mapped to real threats and reviewed regularly detects more.

beginner.definition: Detection use case management means looking after the rules that warn you about attacks. A use case is one specific thing you want to detect, such as a strange login at night. Management means each rule has an owner, a test and a review date. It stops a security team from collecting alerts that nobody understands.
beginner.whyItMatters: A security team can drown in alerts and miss the one that matters. Rules that nobody reviews slowly stop working as systems change. Clear ownership means somebody is responsible when a rule fails or stays silent. Coverage checks show which attacks you cannot see yet. Without this discipline, money goes to new tools while real gaps stay open.
howItWorks: The team picks one behaviour worth detecting, based on threats and past incidents.
They write down what data is needed and what a true alert would look like.
An engineer builds the detection logic and tests it with sample or replayed data.
The use case goes live with a named owner and a written response step.
The team reviews alert counts and false alarms, then tunes or retires the rule.
Managers map all use cases against known attacker methods to find missing coverage.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk that receives many alarms from patient rooms. If every alarm sounds the same and nobody knows which one matters, staff begin to ignore them. A good ward keeps a short list of the alarms that really matter. Staff check each one weekly and remove the ones that only make noise. Detection use case management is that list and that routine for a security team.
takeaways: Every detection rule should have an owner, a test and a review date.
Fewer, well tested rules beat a huge set of untuned alerts.
Map your rules against known attacker methods to find what you cannot see.

objectives: Explain what a detection use case is and how it is managed over time.
Describe the stages of the use case lifecycle from requirement to retirement.
Explain why ownership and documentation matter for detection content.
Describe how alert volume and false positive rate are used to tune a rule.
Explain how coverage mapping reveals gaps in detection.
Identify why a large rule count is a poor measure of maturity.
